Delmer’s deeper idea was this: propaganda tries to force people into a script a role, a language, a way of thinking. The real defense is becoming the author of your own narrative, not an actor repeating someone else’s. (12/12) #informationwarfare #Ukraine

Modern psychological defense is less about consuming more information. It’s about metacognition understanding how your own mind reacts to emotional manipulation, fear, and propaganda. Recognizing when you are being triggered (11/12). #infowar

Another major shift today. The old idea that “more information protects us” no longer works. In a world flooded with content, endless fact-checking can trap people in an information rabbit hole (10/12). #MediaLiteracy #DigitalAge

Real counter-propaganda must also address identity. People leaving radical movements often succeed only when they find a new community to belong to. Without that, they return to the old narrative (9/12).#infowar

That’s why confronting conspiracy believers with facts rarely works. Even when people know information is false, they may still repeat it — because it strengthens their group identity. Facts alone rarely defeat identitym (8/12)  #infowar

Another key lesson: propaganda works because it builds community. Conspiracy theories aren’t just beliefs. They’re social identities an “us vs them” structure that gives people belonging (7/12). #disinformation

Authoritarian systems create internal propaganda ecosystems. In Nazi Germany: SS media attacked the Gestapo. In Russia military bloggers criticize the army. These internal tensions are both a strength and a vulnerability. #russia #disinformation (6/12)

The idea was simple. When ideology is pushed one step further into its own logic, it begins to collapse under its own contradictions. This was not satire or direct criticism. But subtle subversion from inside the narrative. (5/12) #narratives #strategiccommunication

His secret radio stations sounded like Nazi broadcasts. But they were slightly “off”. Often performed by Berlin cabaret artists playing exaggerated Nazi characters pushing the ideology to the point where it became absurd (4/12). #WWII #history

Delmer believed the way to undermine extremist ideology wasn’t attacking it from outside. He entered the enemy’s worldview and twisted it from within. Like putting the left shoe on the right foot: familiar, but deeply uncomfortable.#propaganda #psychologicalwarfare (3/12)

Sefton Delmer, a British journalist turned wartime propagandist, ran clandestine radio operations targeting Nazi Germany. His insight: propaganda isn’t mainly about facts or lies. It’s about identity, the stories people use to understand who they are (2/12)
#infoWar

Intellectual history is a history of intertwining conversations, a history of posing questions not easily—or ever—answered. HIST 271 is a survey of modern European intellectual history, sketching a narrative arc from the late 18th century transition to modernity through the late 20th century transition to post-modernity. (Modernity is largely about replacing God. Postmodernity begins when we give up on replacing God.) With Marci Shore, Associate Professor of History. Please find the reading list for European Intellectual History since Nietzsche, originally taught by Professor Marci Shore in HIST 271/HUMS 339, at the bottom of the page.
